title.en: The World-Tree and the Great Flood (Taulipang, Koch-Grünberg)
title.zh: 世界樹與大洪水（陶利潘格）

region.zh: 羅羅伊馬山陶利潘格-阿雷庫納之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 1-2

summary.en: Makunaima and his brothers suffered great hunger; Aküli the agouti always came home full-bellied, eating in secret the fruits of the wonderful tree Wazakä, which bears every good fruit. Makunaima, watching his lip, found a piece of banana between his teeth, and sent Kali after him. Against the elder brother's warning — 'If you fell the tree, there will be a great water' — the tree was felled with magic words that softened the wood: its stump is today the Roroima itself, and the felled trunks lie across the Caröni as the great falls. Makunaima covered the stump with a basket and let fish come out for the brooks, but lifted the basket a little too high: the water burst out with all its force and threw the basket aside — there was much water, and they could not cover it again. Each brother climbed an Inajä palm to escape the flood; and Aküli, who had hidden in the tree-hole with his fire, still has red hairs on his rump to this day.
summary.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪兄弟饑甚；阿庫利日日飽食而秘之——其私食者乃萬果之樹瓦薩卡也。窺其齒間得蕉，遣卡利隨之。兄誡曰：『伐樹則大水至！』眾以咒言軟其木而伐之——其樁今即羅羅伊馬山，倒木橫卡羅尼河為大灘。馬庫納伊瑪以籃覆樁，縱魚出；稍舉其籃，水暴發不可復塞。兄弟各登伊納雅棕避洪；阿庫利匿樹洞以火自暖，至今臀有赤毛。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth told by Aküli/Mayüluaipu to Koch-Grünberg 1911-12, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Makunaima and his brothers suffered great hunger. Aküli came always home with a full belly: he ate the fruits of the tree Pupü, which he had found in the forest, and said nothing of it to the others; the others ate only the bad fruits of the Kaui-yeg. Makunaima watched him, lifted his lip while he slept, and found a piece of fruit between his teeth. Aküli hid the ripe fruits that lay on the ground in a hole in the trunk and stopped the hole with beeswax.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest brother gave his brothers the advice not to fell this tree again, but only to eat the fruits that fell; Makunaima however wanted to fell it with all his might. The tree Wazakä was tangled with lianas; Makunaima sent Kali up to cut them, but many wasps there stung him in the eyelids — hence they are swollen to this day. Makunaima hacked on one side of the trunk with his magic word and it grew ever softer, while the eldest brother hacked the other side with his, and it grew ever harder: the tree broke and fell — its stump is today the Roroima; the fallen trunks lie across the Caröni and form the high falls over which boats must be unloaded and hauled overland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest brother covered the stump of Wazakä with a basket; out of the stump came many fish. When the stump was covered Makunaima said: 'Let a little more fish come out for these brooks; then we will cover the stump.' He lifted the basket a little — the water came with all its force and threw the basket quite aside: much water came out, and they could not cover it again. Makunaima stuck a very tall Inajä stem into the earth to save himself from the flood, and each brother climbed his own palm. Aküli had crawled into the hole of the trunk where he had hidden his bananas; he made a fire in the hole and warmed himself — the fire seized his rump and turned into red hairs: to this day Aküli has red hairs on his rump.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 1; not verbatim.

narrative.en: Among the Taulipang and Arekuna Carib-speaking peoples of the Roroima (Roraima) region, the cycle that explains the whole habitable world begins with hunger and ends with mountains. Makunaima — the youngest of a set of brothers but the craftiest — and his brothers are starving. Aküli, the agouti, comes home every evening with a full belly, and the brothers eat only the poor fruits of the Kaui-yeg tree. Makunaima's suspicion is proven in a small and vivid way: while Aküli sleeps he lifts his lip and finds a fragment of banana, Wazakä-püu, between his teeth. Spies are sent after the hoarder; wasps sting the eyelids of the first, Kali, whose swollen eyelids every one of his kind has carried since. At last the eldest brother brings back a full back-basket and confesses. Aküli, who is clever and knows everything beforehand, begs them to leave the great tree Wazakä standing: 'If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!' But the axe is guided by magic words — one brother chops a side soft, another chops his side hard, until the tree breaks. It falls toward the north, which is why the wild banana groves of that country belong not to men but to the Mauari, the mountain demons; and the standing stump is today the mountain Roroima itself, while the felled trunks lie across the Caröni river as its impassable cataracts. Out of the stump pours water and great fish. A basket is set over the stump to hold back the flood, but Makunaima, wanting a few more fish for the brooks, lifts it: the water bursts out with all its force and can never be stopped again. Each brother plants an Inajä palm-stem and climbs it as the world drowns; Aküli hides in the hollow of the trunk with his fire and warms himself — the fire catches his rump and turns to red hairs, which every agouti still wears. After the flood a second destruction follows, the Sinbrand or world-fire, and Makunaima then attempts the re-creation of mankind: first of wax, which melts in the sun, then of clay, which hardens in it — and from the hardened clay he transforms the people of to-day. The tale is told in one line or the other by the Arekuna shaman Aküli (mock-named for the agouti) and the Taulipang Mayüluaipu, who dictated it to Theodor Koch-Grünberg at camp-fires and on the river during his 1911-12 expedition, and stands as the Taulipang twin of the wider Guianese cycle of the wonderful tree whose stump becomes a mountain and whose waters become the flood.

functions: Explains the physical geography of the Pakaraima region: Roroima as the tree-stump, the Caröni falls as felled trunks, wild banana groves as the property of the mountain demons Mauari
Authorises the shaman's authority: the narrative is told by medicine-men, whose predecessors like Aküli 'know everything beforehand' and see the Mauari

Provides the calendar and subsistence frame: the flood explains the distribution of fish (abundant on the far side of the Roroima), and the cycle continues into fire, the making of people from clay, and the origin of hunting animals
Marks transgression: Aküli's concealment, Kali's disobedience, Makunaima's impatient lifting of the basket each leave permanent signs on the bodies of animals and men

variants.name: Arekuna version (Aküli)
variants.summary: The agouti found the tree Pupü first, and only later the great Wazakä; the brothers had no fire yet and took it from the small bird Mutüg by tying a cord to his tail; Aküli's rump reddens in the fire he lit inside the trunk-hole.

variants.name: Akawai version (Brett)
variants.summary: Makunaima's son rules the one-speech animals; the agouti Ahkoo finds the tree; the monkey Iwarreka, banished to fetch water, lifts the basket over the stump and releases the flood; the survivors climb a cocorite hill.

variants.name: Carib version (im Thurn)
variants.text_tradition: True Carib, recorded by im Thurn 1883
variants.summary: After descending from sky-land the Caribs find all food on one huge tree; the tapir discovers it, the woodpecker spoils the stalking, the rat leads to it; from the stump a flood flows and is stopped by an inverted basket — until the brown monkey raises it.

title.en: Ma'ndpe the Accursed Fells the World-Tree (Taulipang)
title.zh: 受咒者曼德佩伐世界樹

region.zh: 羅羅伊馬山陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 2

summary.en: In ancient time five brothers lived at the foot of the Roroima: Makunaima, Ma'ndpe, Anzikilan, Wakalaimbe and Anike. Aküli, then a human being, found deep in the forest the giant tree Wazakä, bearing every kind of banana, papaya, cashew, orange and maize, and told no one. Makunaima found the banana-fragment between his sleeping teeth; Kali stung by wasps came home with swollen eyelids; at last the eldest brother brought a full back-basket home and told everything. 'Tomorrow we will fell the tree!' said Ma'ndpe, the accursed. Aküli, who was very clever and knew everything beforehand, said: 'No, we will not fell it! If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!' But Ma'ndpe was stubborn, took an axe and hacked the trunk, saying the magic words that made the wood ever softer; Aküli warned again and again, taking every fruit-skin and beeswax to stop at once the holes Ma'ndpe hacked. The tree fell toward the other side of the Roroima, and many bananas fell there — that is why there are banana groves in the forest to-day that no one planted; they belong to the Mauari, the mountain demons, whose houses all the mountains there are, as the shamans say, who alone can see and speak with the Mauari. Much water pressed out of the tree, and many very great fish came out — but all went to the other side; there are still very many great fish there, and on this side only few and small.
summary.zh: 昔羅羅伊馬山下有五兄弟。阿庫利覓得巨樹瓦薩卡，百果具備而秘之。馬庫納伊瑪窺其齒；卡利為蜂螫而瞼腫；長兄負蕉滿筐而歸，盡告其事。曼德佩曰：『明日伐樹！』阿庫利豫知曰：『毋伐！伐則大水至！』曼德佩固執，以咒軟其木而斧之；阿庫利以果皮蜂蠟塞其斧穴。樹倒於山之彼側，蕉林遍布——今之野蕉林，皆屬山鬼毛阿利；薩滿獨能見之與言。水自樹出，巨魚隨湧——然皆往彼側；故彼處大魚極多，此側則稀而小。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth told by Mayüluaipu to Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In ancient time five brothers lived at the foot of the Roroima: Makunaima, Ma'ndpe, Anzikilan, Wakalaimbe and Anike. These five brothers had great hunger and nothing to eat. Aküli, who in ancient time was a human being, found deep in the forest a giant tree, Wazakä, which bore every good fruit — all kinds of banana, papaya, cashew, orange, maize. He ate of it every day, but said nothing to the people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Makunaima lifted Aküli's lip as he slept and found a piece of banana Wazakä-püu between his teeth. Kali climbed the tree against Aküli's warning and was stung in the upper eyelids by two wasps — since that time Kali has swollen eyelids. At last Ma'ndpe ate many bananas till his belly was full, filled his back-basket, and told his brother everything. 'Tomorrow we will fell the tree!' said Ma'ndpe, the accursed. Aküli, who was very clever and knew everything beforehand, said: 'No, we will not fell it! We will only gather fruits! If you fell the tree, there will be a great water!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Ma'ndpe was stubborn, took an axe and hacked the trunk, saying the magic words; the wood became ever softer, and the axe bit ever deeper. Aküli warned still: 'Fell it not! Fell it not! Else comes much water!' He took all fruit-skins and beeswax and stopped at once all the holes Ma'ndpe hacked. The tree fell toward the other side of the Roroima, and many bananas fell there — therefore there are to-day banana groves in the forest which no one planted, and they belong to the Mauari (mountain demons): all the mountains there, Roroima and others, are their houses, so say the shamans, who alone can see the Mauari and speak with them. Much water pressed out of the tree, and many very great fish came out — but all went to the other side; there are still very many great fish there, and on this side only few and small.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Sinbrand: the Fire That Came After the Flood
title.zh: 天火：洪水之後焚世之焰

region.zh: 羅羅伊馬陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 3-4

summary.en: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth — no one knows where that hole stayed. It burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones. The rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth. Makunaima made new people out of wax — but these melted quite away in the sun. Then he made people out of clay; these grew ever harder in the sun. Then he transformed them into human beings.
summary.zh: 大水之後，萬物既燥，天火至焉。百獸穿地穴而遁——穴在何處，無人知也。火焚一切：人、山、石皆燼；諸河盡涸——故地下至今猶得巨炭。馬庫納伊瑪以蠟造新人；日光之下盡融。乃以泥造人；日曬愈堅。遂化而為人。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth — no one knows where that hole stayed. It burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones. The rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: After the great flood, when everything was dry, a great fire came. All the wild creatures slipped through a hole into the earth; no one knows where that hole stayed. The fire burned everything: the people, the mountains, the stones; the rivers dried up; therefore one still finds great pieces of coal in the earth to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 3; not verbatim.

title.en: The Deeds of Makunaima: Men, Beasts, and the Singing Stone
title.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪之功業：人獸化石與鳴石

region.zh: 蘇魯米河陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 4-6

summary.en: Makunaima went to the other side of the Roroima, where he probably still lives to-day, and transformed men and women into rocks, as well as saüba ants, tapirs and wild swine: a rock near Koimelemong is a pig that sticks its head into the earth; at the Aruayä Mountains is a great pot with a basket inverted over it; at the Serra do Mel a hunting-bag turned to stone. A man had stolen a piece of urucü from Makunaima; Makunaima followed his trail, caught him, cut off his head, arms and legs, and transformed everything into stones, as one still sees them on a savanna of the Mairari Mountains — the savanna is called Anuntä-lemon, the 'urucü savanna'. There too stands a woman with her rump in the air, all parts visible. A Mutum bird is also to be seen close by: when a human being is going to die, the stone sings like a Mutum. Makunaima made all the hunting animals and fish. Then he met people who did not want to believe in the great water of which he had told them, and who wanted to go home: when they turned around he transformed them all into termite mounds, as many are still found on the side of the Mairari Mountains.
summary.zh: 馬庫納伊瑪越羅羅伊馬而居彼側，至今猶在。化男女為石，蟻、貘、野豬亦然：科伊梅勒蒙附近之石乃豬首入地者；阿魯雅揚山有大釜覆籃；賽拉多梅爾有石化獵囊。一人竊其烏魯庫；追而擒之，斬首截肢，盡化為石——其草原今名『烏魯庫草原』。又有婦石，臀翹而全形畢露。旁有穆通鳥之石：人將死時，石如穆通而鳴。凡獸與魚皆其所造。不信大水者，回首之頃盡化為白蟻塚。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Makunaima went to the other side of the Roroima and probably still lives there to-day. He transformed there men and women into rocks, as well as saübas, tapirs and wild swine: a rock near Koimelemong is a pig that sticks its head into the earth; at the Aruayä Mountains is found a great pot over which a basket is inverted; at the Serra do Mel a hunting-bag transformed into stone.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: A man had stolen a piece of urucü from Makunaima; Makunaima followed his trail, caught him, cut off his head, arms and legs, and transformed everything into stones, as one still sees them on a savanna of the Mairari Mountains — the savanna is called from it Anuntä-lemon, the 'urucü savanna'. There too is seen a woman with her rump in the air, all parts visible. A Mutum is also to be seen close by: when a human being is going to die, the stone sings like a Mutum.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he met the people who did not want to believe in the great water of which he had told them, and who wanted to go home. He said to them: 'Whither do you want to go?' When they turned around, he transformed them all into termite mounds, as many are still found on the side of the Mairari Mountains. Makunaima made all the hunting animals and fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.

title.en: Makunaima the Aimarä Fish: the Stolen Fishing-Hook

region.zh: 羅羅伊馬諸河陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 5-6

summary.en: Then all the rivers dried up, and the fish stayed in the lakes and little brooks, and there was abundance of fish. Makunaima made fishing-hooks out of beeswax, but caught nothing, for when the fish bit they bit the hook in two. So he met a man who was fishing for Aimarä. 'What shall we do? We will steal his hook! I will transform myself into an Aimarä, and if he catches me and hauls me out I shall cheat him: when he strikes me on the head I shall make a mess and pretend to die. Brother, ask him for that fish to eat! I shall become the biggest Aimarä there is.' He sprang into the water, became the biggest Aimarä, and bit; the man hauled him out, struck him on the head, drew the hook from his mouth; the brother begged the fish, recognised it by its closed eyes, took it home — and it became Makunaima again. A second time he became a Piränya and snapped the hook away. When the man had gone off to work on the other side, the two brothers transformed themselves into crickets and sat in his back-basket, and so came over to the other side — where Makunaima and the eldest still live to-day. In the basket Makunaima conjured wounds upon his body, pulled them off, threw them on the path and transformed them into stones: 'Remain here! To all people who walk this path you shall cling!' — that is why people who walk this path suffer from wounds to this day.
summary.zh: 諸河既涸，魚聚湖沼，魚豐。馬庫納伊瑪以蜂蠟為釣鉤，無所得——魚齧即齧斷其鉤。乃化為大特拉希拉魚上鉤；人曳之出、擊其首，彼佯死；兄索魚而歸，魚復為馬庫納伊瑪。再化皮拉尼亞，齧斷其鉤。人往彼岸作工，兄弟化蟋蟀匿其背籃而同渡——至今居彼。籃中馬庫納伊瑪咒傷於身，摘而擲於道，化為石：『留此！凡行此道者，爾等附之！』故行此道者至今身多瘡傷。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Then all the rivers dried up, and the fish stayed in the lakes and little brooks, and there was abundance of fish. Makunaima made fishing-hooks out of beeswax, but caught nothing, for when the fish bit, they bit the fishing-hook in two. So he met a man who was fishing for Aimarä.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What shall we do? We will steal his hook! I will transform myself into an Aimarä and steal the hook from him. If he catches me and hauls me out, I shall cheat him: if he strikes me on the head, I shall make a mess and pretend to die. Brother, ask him for this fish to eat! I shall become the biggest Aimarä there is.' He sprang into the water, transformed himself into the biggest Aimarä and bit; the man hauled him out, struck him on the head, drew the hook from his mouth. The brother begged the fish, knew him by his closed eyes, took the fish with him — and it transformed itself again into Makunaima.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: The man went away to work on the other side, making manioc cakes for the journey. 'We will transform ourselves into crickets and sit in his back-basket!' They transformed themselves into crickets and sat in his basket, and so came to the other side, where Makunaima and the eldest brother still live to-day. In the basket Makunaima conjured wounds on his body and said: 'I am tired of these wounds! I will pull them off!' He pulled them off, threw them on the path and transformed them into stones: 'Remain here! To all people who walk this path you shall cling!' — that is why people who walk this path suffer from wounds to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 5; not verbatim.

title.en: Akalapizeima and the Sun: Why We Grow Old
title.zh: 阿卡拉皮澤瑪與日神：人之所以老

region.zh: 卡羅尼河阿雷庫納之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 13

summary.en: In ancient time there was a very tall tree, which Walo'mä, the toad, climbed quite to the top. A man named Akalapizeima lurked every afternoon at the foot of the tree to catch her. 'If Akalapizeima catches me, I shall throw him into the sea!' She caught him by the hands, pushed him with her foot into the sea, loaded him on her back and swam with him to an island, where she left him under a tree on which carrion vultures sat; while he slept they covered him quite with their droppings. It was very cold on the island, and the man froze. The Morning Star would not take him up — 'you gave cassava cakes only ever to the Sun'; the Moon refused him too. Then came Wüi, the Sun, to whom he had given many cassava cakes: she took him into her boat, had him washed by her daughters, and wanted him for a son-in-law: 'You shall marry one of my daughters, but do not let yourself in with another woman!' Wüi stopped at a maloka; he went ashore anyway, met the daughters of the carrion vulture and fell in love with them. The daughters of the Sun scolded him; Wüi grew angry: 'Had you followed my counsel and married one of my daughters, you would have remained young and beautiful for ever like me. Now you remain young and beautiful only a short time; then you will grow old and ugly!' They slept; in the morning Wüi went away with his daughters and left Akalapizeima asleep: he found himself among the vultures, old and ugly, as Wüi had said. He married a daughter of the vulture and got used to the life. He was our forefather, the father of all Indians — that is why we remain young and handsome only a short time, and then become old and ugly.
summary.zh: 上古有巨樹；蟾蜍瓦洛瑪攀其顛。獵者阿卡拉皮澤瑪候樹下欲捕之；蟾言：『彼捕我，我必擲之於海！』遂執其手，以足踢入海，負之游至孤島，置於禿鷲樹下；鷲屎淋之。島寒甚。晨星不援——『爾薯餅惟供日也』；月亦拒之。日神惠伊至——彼薯餅多供於日——乃載之於舟，令諸女為之浴，欲妻以女：『娶我女，毋戀他女！』泊於屋而登岸；遇禿鷲諸女而戀之。日神怒曰：『若聽我言而娶我女，則恆如我之少且美；今爾美少不久，必老而醜！』晨惠伊攜女去；彼醒而處鷲群之中，老而醜矣。娶鷲女而安其生——彼即吾儕之祖，眾印第安人之父：故吾人少美不久，而老醌隨之。

sensitivity.note: Arekuna myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In ancient time there was a very tall tree, which Walo'mä, the toad, climbed quite to the top. A man, named Akalapizeima, lurked every afternoon at the foot of the tree to catch Walo'mä. 'If Akalapizeima catches me, I shall throw him into the sea!' The man caught her; she seized him by the hands, pushed him with her foot into the sea, loaded him on her back, dove under and swam with him to an island. There she left him and swam back; she left him under a tree on which carrion vultures sat, which covered him quite with droppings while he slept.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was very cold on the island, and the man froze very much. Kaiuanög, the Morning Star, met him: 'I cannot take you up. You have given me nothing; you have only always given the Sun cassava cakes.' The Moon also refused him. Then came Wüi, the Sun. She took him into her boat, had him washed by her daughters and his hair cut, and made him beautiful again. Wüi wanted him for a son-in-law: 'You shall marry one of my daughters, but do not let yourself in with another woman!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wüi stopped at a maloka and went ashore with her daughters; he went ashore anyway, met some young girls, the daughters of the carrion vulture, and fell in love with them. The daughters of the Sun scolded him; Wüi grew angry: 'If you had followed my counsel and married one of my daughters, you would have remained always young and beautiful as I. Now you remain only a short time young and beautiful; then you will become old and ugly!' In the morning Wüi drove away with her daughters and left Akalapizeima sleeping; when he awoke he found himself among the vultures, old and ugly, as Wüi had said. He married a daughter of the vulture and got used to the life. He was our forefather, the father of all Indians. Therefore we live to-day in this condition: we remain only a short time young and handsome, and then become old and ugly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 13; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Moon Went Up to Heaven: the Liana Ladder and the Road of the Dead
title.zh: 月升天記：藤梯與亡者之路

region.zh: 羅羅伊馬陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 14-15

summary.en: In ancient time Kapei, the Moon, was not in the sky but on the earth, and had a house here. He seized the soul of a child, put it into a pot and turned the pot upside down on the ground: the child fell sick, and a shaman was called to blow upon it in the night. Kapei hid in another great pot and bade his two grown daughters not betray where he was. The shaman forced into the house, smashed the pot, found the soul of the child, seized Kapei, thrashed him through, and drove him out: 'Stay here no longer! Go away from here!' Then Kapei thought where he should live. 'Cutia is eaten! Tapir is eaten! Wild swine is eaten! All the hunting animals are eaten! If I transform myself into a bird — a Mutüm? A Cujubim? They too are eaten! I go to heaven! It is better there than here! I will go, to shine for my brothers there below. Let us go, my daughters, to heaven!' They made a liana, Kapeyenkumä(x)pe, like a ladder, to climb up; a little bird from heaven carried one end up and tied it at the entrance of heaven; Kapei and his daughters climbed the liana into the sky. 'I remain here in heaven! Go higher, to light the way! I remain here to shine for my brothers below. You shall light the way for the people who die, so that the shadow may not remain in the dark!' He sent one daughter higher to another heaven, the other still higher to another heaven; he himself remained in the heaven above us — above our heaven, the Taulipang believe, are yet ten more heavens, one above the other.
summary.zh: 上古月神卡佩伊居地上，有屋焉。奪小兒之魂，納於釜而倒置之；兒病，召薩滿夜吹療之。卡佩伊匿於大釜，囑二女毋洩。薩滿破釜得魂，執卡佩伊痛毆而逐之：『毋復居此！去！』卡佩伊自思：『獸皆可食，鳥亦可食；天則勝此！吾往天，為吾兄弟下界而光。』乃結藤梯卡佩延庫馬佩，遣小鳥繫其端於天門；父女攀藤而升。『我居天！爾等升而照亡者之路，俾魂不滯黑暗！』遣一女更高之天，又遣一女更上之天；己居吾儕之上天——陶利潘格人言其上尚有十天，層層相疊。

Kapei was at enmity with the people. Kapei had two grown daughters; he hid in another great pot and bade his daughters turn the pot over him: 'Betray not where I am when the shaman comes! Betray not either where the child is!'

He pressed into the house, smashed the pot with his club, then smashed the other pot too, and so found the soul of the child. He found also Kapei, who had hidden in the pot; he seized Kapei, thrashed him through, drove him out of the house and said: 'Stay here no longer! Go away from here!'

title.en: How the Moon Got His Dirty Face (Taulipang)

region.zh: 阿雷庫納-陶利潘格之地

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 15

summary.en: Wüi and Kapëi, Sun and Moon, were in ancient time friends and went together. Kapëi was then very beautiful and had a clear face. He fell in love with a daughter of Wüi and consorted with her every night. But Wüi would not have it, and bade his daughter smear menstrual blood over Kapëi's face. Since that time they are enemies: Kapëi always goes far from Wüi, and is to this day quite dirty in the face.
summary.zh: 昔惠伊與卡佩伊相友而行。卡佩伊甚美，面明淨；戀惠伊之女，夜夜與之私。惠伊不許，命其女以經血塗卡佩伊之面。自此二人為仇：卡佩伊恆遠避惠伊，至今面垢如故。

sensitivity.note: Arekuna myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Wüi and Kapëi, Sun and Moon, were in ancient time friends and went together. Kapëi was then very beautiful and had a clear face. He fell in love with a daughter of Wüi and gave himself up with her every night. But Wüi would not have it, and bade his daughter smear menstrual blood over Kapëi's face. Since that time they are enemies: Kapëi always goes far from Wüi and is to this day quite dirty in the face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 15; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon and His Two Wives

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 16-17

summary.en: Kapëi, the Moon, has two wives, who are both called Kayuanög, one in the east, the other in the west — the two planets Venus and Jupiter. He is always with one wife: first he goes with the one who gives him much to eat, so that he grows ever fatter; then he leaves her and goes with the other, who gives him only little to eat, so that he grows leaner from day to day; then he meets the other again, who makes him fat again, and so on. The wife in the east quarrels with the Moon out of jealousy: 'Go to the other wife! Then you will grow fat again; with me you will not grow fat!' And he goes to the other. Therefore both wives are enemies and remain always far from each other. The wife who makes him fat said: 'This shall remain for ever the custom of these people!' — therefore many Taulipang and Makuschi have three or four wives. At sun- or moon-eclipse Olo'zän, who was formerly a human being and is now a demon in human form, strikes Wüi or Kapëi in the face with a club, so that blood flows over and the face darkens: it is a sign that there is war.
summary.zh: 月有二妻，皆名卡尤阿諾格，一東一西——即金星與木星也。月常與一妻偕：與肥妻則日胖；離而就瘦妻則日瘦；復遇肥妻而復胖，如是循環。東妻妒而詈曰：『往就彼妻！爾將復胖；於我則不能胖也！』月遂往。二妻因此為仇，永不相近。肥妻曰：『此俗當永為此人間之制！』故陶利潘格與馬庫希人多有三四妻。日月蝕之時，奧洛贊——昔為人今為人形之魔——以棍擊日或月之面，血流而面晦：此戰亂之兆也。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myths recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

title.en: Tamekan, the One-Legged Man of the Pleiades

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 18-19

summary.en: Tamekän is a man with only one leg; the other was hacked off him on earth. Zilizoaibu had a wife, Wayülalë, who cared nothing for him but loved his handsome brother. Picking abacate-fruits up a tree, he was followed by his wife, who had secretly brought an axe: as he climbed down, halfway up the trunk, she hacked off his right leg. The little bird Koezäg sang to the brother in the plantation: 'His brother's leg his wife hacked off with the axe!' The brother ran home in fury; the wife wrapped him fast in the hammock so that he could not help, while the wounded man lay outside crying till midnight. Then the cripple raised himself at the doorpost, climbed the roof, and played on his reed flute 'tin-tin-tin'; and he spoke to his brother: 'Remain in the house! Raise good sons and good daughters! Good health and luck! I go away — but beware of the wife and mistrust her always!' — 'Whither goest thou?' — 'I go to heaven! I will be Tamekän, a body with one leg that remains behind!' The Pleiades are the head, the Aldebaran group the body, and Orion the leg that remained. When Tamekän went to heaven, always fluting 'tin-tin-tin', the wife released the brother; and he vowed revenge: catching her head in a hollow bee-tree, he thrust her in and sealed the hole — 'What you did to my brother you shall now pay me!' She cried for her children, made 'kenön-kenön' like an armadillo, and remained transformed into an armadillo. Later the father led his five children deep into the forest, burned the house behind them, and said: 'We will become Araiuäg, for these they do not kill and eat!' — and they vanished one behind the other into the forest; that is why the Araiuäg loves honey to this day, and fears no bees.
summary.zh: 塔梅坎者，獨腿人也；其腿在世為妻所斫。齊利佐伊布之妻惠雅拉勒不愛其夫而愛其弟。夫攀果樹，妻懷斧隨之；及降，半樹而斫其右腿。小鳥告其弟：『兄之腿，妻以斧斫之！』弟怒歸；妻裹之於吊床不得救，而傷者臥外哀號至半夜。傷者攀屋頂，吹葦笛『叮叮叮』，謂弟曰：『居家！育善子女！我往天，將為塔梅坎——獨腿之軀也！』昴宿乃其首，畢宿為其身，獵戶為其餘腿。妻聞笛而釋弟；弟復仇，誘妻首入空心蜂樹而封之——『爾所為吾兄者，今償於我！』妻呼其兒，作犰狳聲，遂化為犰狳。後父攜五子入深林，焚屋於後，曰：『吾儕將為阿拉伊瓦格——人不殺不食者也！』相繼隱於林；故阿拉伊瓦格至今嗜蜜而無懼於蜂。

sensitivity.note: Taulipang myth recorded by Koch-Grünberg, publ. 1924; archival record, read critically.

Picking abacate-fruits, Zilizoaibu climbed the tree; she had secretly brought an axe, gathered the fruits he threw down, and waited only for the moment when he came down: as he was halfway up the trunk she took the axe and hacked off his right leg, as one still sees to-day. She returned to the house.

Wayülalë lay in the hammock, gave him cassiri, and when night came wrapped him in the hammock so fast that he could not get out — not even to piss. The wounded man lay outside and cried with pain till midnight: 'O my brother, my leg is hacked off with the axe! Kill this woman!' But the wife did not let the brother out of the hammock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.

Raise good sons and good daughters! Good health and luck! I go away. Raise a good family, but beware of the wife and mistrust her always!' — 'Whither goest thou?' — 'I go to heaven! I will be Tamekän, a body with one leg that remains behind!' The Pleiades are the head, the Aldebaran group the body, and Orion the leg that remained. Until this day Tamekän announces the winter: when he has gone to heaven there is much thunder and rain, the fish-shoals come, and you will eat many fish.

passages.text: The younger brother remained with the wife, made house and plantation, and had with her five children. One day, going hunting, he found a bee-nest; leading her to it, he coaxed her to thrust her head into the hollow to gather the honey — and thrust her quite in with the piece of wood he had hewn out, sealing the hole. 'What you did to my brother you shall now pay me! You shall suffer what my brother suffered! I am very sorry for you, wife, but I can no longer bear what you did to my brother!' She cried at first aloud: 'My poor children! My poor children! Even if I am transformed into an armadillo, I shall always remember my children!' Then she cried ever softer, made 'kenön-kenön-kenön' like the armadillo, and remained transformed into an armadillo. Later the father led his five children deep into the forest, burned the house behind them, and said: 'We will become Araiuäg, for these they do not kill and eat!' — and they vanished one behind the other into the forest; therefore the Araiuäg loves honey to this day and has no fear of the bees.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Koch-Grünberg 1924, Mythe 18; not verbatim.

title.en: Zilizoaibu and the Crystal Stones: the Origin of the Piranhas
title.zh: 齊利佐伊布與水晶石：皮拉魚之由

source.work: Theodor Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roraima zum Orinoco, Bd. II: Mythen und Legenden der Taulipang- und Arekuna-Indianer (1924), Mythe 19

summary.en: The mother-in-law of Zilizoaibu gave her son-in-law Käliwaü fish to eat: she set an old calabash under herself and pressed her belly together, whereupon the fish came out of her uterus and fell into the calabash — that is why the Taulipang do not eat this fish to this day. The old woman bade him make a fish-trap, to make him believe she caught the fish with it; but the son-in-law, being a shaman, knew everything. He broke many crystal stones, such as are found at the Roroima, cut a leaf from the 'wild banana' and covered with it the stones at the river place where the old woman always went down and pressed the fish out of her uterus. When she went down to the landing she slipped on the stones and fell: the sharp stones cut her arms and legs and her whole body into little pieces, so that she died; the stones ate the flesh to the bones, then plunged into the river and transformed themselves into Arai — piranha fish — which eat people to this day. The liver of the old woman, cut by the stones, remained swimming on the water: one still sees it; the Taulipang call it Elima, the Brazilians Mureru brava — a water-plant with red leaves — and the heart of the old woman remained in the middle of the leaves: it is the heart-shaped seed of the plant.
summary.zh: 齊利佐伊布之岳母以卡利瓦伊魚饗其婿：置舊葫蘆於身下，壓其腹；魚自子宮出而落於葫蘆——故陶利潘格人至今不食此魚。老嫗令其婿製魚籠，詭稱以此捕魚；然婿為薩滿，盡知之。乃碎水晶石——羅羅伊馬所產也——以野蕉葉覆之於老嫗常臨之灘。嫻至灘而滑倒；利石碎其肢體，逐段食其肉，遂死；石飽而躍入河，化為皮拉尼亞——至今食人。其肝浮於水，至今可見：陶利潘格名之艾利馬，巴西人名穆雷魯布拉瓦——紅葉水草也——其心在葉心，即草之心形種子。
